analysis.one_liner: Phases out nonessential "forever chemicals" from manufacturing, releases, and everyday products.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with no cosponsors in March 2026 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force manufacturers and users of PFAS — the long-lasting "forever chemicals" found in nonstick coatings, water-repellent fabrics, food packaging, and many industrial processes — to report their use each year and stop all nonessential uses within ten years. It bans PFAS in a long list of consumer products on faster timelines (carpets and food packaging within a year, cosmetics and indoor furniture within two, and so on), and after ten years makes it illegal to release PFAS into the environment at any detectable level. It gives the EPA enforcement tools including civil and criminal penalties, lets citizens sue violators, and addresses state lawsuits over PFAS exposure, including bankruptcy rules that keep companies from shielding allied entities from cleanup claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people exposed to PFAS through drinking water, food packaging, clothing, carpets, and cosmetics; communities near contaminated sites, who get mandatory public notice and meetings when an imminent hazard is found; and people pursuing damages lawsuits over PFAS exposure, since the bill addresses state-law claims and statutes of repose and keeps bankruptcy from blocking claims against non-debtor companies.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers and users must report PFAS uses, volumes, releases at any detectable level, exposure of workers, and health effects, with reports published for public comment — creating public transparency about where the chemicals are and who is exposed.

Nonessential uses of PFAS must be fully phased out within ten years, with faster deadlines for specific products: carpets, rugs, fabric treatments, food packaging, and juvenile products within one year; cosmetics, indoor textiles, furniture, and apparel within two; outdoor furnishings within four; and outdoor severe-wet-weather gear within five.

Ten years after enactment it becomes unlawful to release any PFAS above the threshold of detection, and the EPA gets authority to inspect facilities, require monitoring, and impose civil penalties designed to strip out the economic benefit of violations, plus criminal penalties including up to five years' imprisonment.
Any person can sue manufacturers, users, or the EPA over violations or imminent endangerment, with courts able to award attorney and expert witness fees.

The bill addresses state-law damages actions for hazardous-substance exposure, including statutes of repose, and exempts from bankruptcy's automatic stay any proceeding against a non-debtor entity on a claim involving persistent, bioaccumulative, toxic chemicals — making it harder for companies to escape PFAS cleanup and damages liability through corporate restructuring.

Federal agencies must eliminate procurement of products known to contain PFAS to the maximum extent practicable, and the government waives immunity so federal facilities must comply with federal, state, and local PFAS laws, with a narrow national-security exemption the President must report to Congress and generally make public.

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers and the industries that put PFAS in consumer goods — textiles, carpets, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture, and oil and gas products — bear reformulation, reporting, and compliance costs, some of which could show up as higher prices. Taxpayers fund the EPA's enforcement program and the National Academies review, which are authorized to be appropriated such sums as necessary.

drawbacks.text: Reformulating products without PFAS costs money, and compliance or product changes could be passed to consumers as higher prices for everyday goods like clothing, furniture, and cosmetics.

The bill sets up a fee system for annual reports and essential-use petitions, with a required minimum of $100,000 per report or petition if the EPA misses its two-year rulemaking deadline — a fee the EPA may lower for small manufacturers but is not required to.

The essential-use designation depends on a National Academies review that may not conclude until three years after it begins, and no designations can be finalized before the first report after that review — meaning industry could argue the process is slow and uncertain for uses it considers critical, even though uses truly critical to health and safety can be designated essential with no safer alternative available.

A release ban at the level of detection is stricter than typical pollution limits, and regulated industries would argue it is technologically demanding and costly to meet, even with the ten-year lead time and a rulemaking to establish validated detection methods.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health case is strong: PFAS persist in the environment and in the human body, and exposure is widespread through drinking water and everyday products. The bill protects the genuinely critical uses (medical, safety-critical uses can be designated essential) and gives industry years to transition, while the main real costs are reformulation expenses, possible price increases, and litigation exposure for companies that caused contamination. The bill is broadly written and its timelines depend heavily on EPA follow-through, but the trade-off — cleaner water and fewer exposures versus compliance costs on a well-documented toxic pollutant — favors the public side.

outcome.mechanism: Durbin introduced the bill alone and it went straight to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which has not held any action on it since.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 19, 2026, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
No other senator has signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee has taken no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote appears in the bill's action history.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the companies that make and use PFAS, and the members who can leave the bill unactioned in committee, since no phaseout obligation exists without a law.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.role: U.S. Senator from Illinois; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.role: Committee of referral; has not acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no further action — no hearing or vote is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or committee action have occurred, so the partisan shape is unknown; so far the bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill phases out nonessential PFAS production within ten years, bans releases at any detectable level, and exposes violators to civil and criminal penalties and citizen suits. The industry's interest in avoiding these mandates runs directly against the public's interest in less exposure to persistent toxic chemicals.

industries.industry: Consumer product makers (textiles, carpets, cosmetics, food packaging, furniture)
industries.note: The bill bans the sale of PFAS-containing products in these categories on one- to five-year timelines, forcing reformulation. Their compliance costs are the price of removing a persistent chemical from products that touch people's skin, food, and homes.
Oil and gas products containing PFAS face a one-year sales ban. The industry's cost here is the public's gain in reduced release of the chemicals.

industries.industry: Water utilities and waste treatment operators
industries.note: The bill explicitly excludes public water systems, solid waste and composting facilities, and treatment works from the definitions of manufacturer and user, since they only passively receive PFAS. That shields ratepayer-funded utilities from liability as polluters, though utilities still bear the cost of treating contaminated water.

industries.industry: PFAS litigation plaintiffs and their counsel
industries.note: The bill addresses state-law damages actions, including statutes of repose, and exempts proceedings against non-debtor entities from bankruptcy's automatic stay for toxic-chemical claims — strengthening the hand of people suing over exposure damages.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no committee action since referral in a Senate where the bill's party is in the minority, the realistic path is that the bill stays in committee and expires at the end of this Congress, as most single-sponsor bills without cross-party support do. Moving it would require other senators — especially from the majority party — to sign on and the committee to schedule work.
